title: 35 Byproduct feeds and interseeded red clover as supplemental diets affecting animal performance in ‘KY31’ tall fescue pastures
content:
Abstract
‘KY31’ tall fescue (Schedonorus arundinaceus), while a persistent and productive forage in the Southeast, causes significant economic losses to the US beef industry due to symptoms like poor animal performance. Current methods for mitigating this problem or prohibitively expensive such as mixing with other grass and legume species to dilute ergot alkaloid intake or transitioning to novel-endophyte tall fescue, making them unfeasible for most beef cattle producers in the Southeast. Thus, our overall objective was to identify supplemental feeding programs, using byproduct feedstuffs and interseeded red clover (Trifolium pretense), to economically support beef cattle production and mitigate fescue toxicosis. The experiment was conducted on replicated ‘KY31’ tall fescue pastures at Black Belt Research and Extension Center (BBREC; n = 8), and Tennessee Valley Research and Extension Center (TVREC; n = 12). Pre-conditioned stocker steers (267 ± 35.8 kg BW), sourced from a private contractor, were used in a generalized complete block design. Steers were randomly assigned based on body weight to replicate pastures (1 ha) which were randomly allocated to 1 of 4 supplementation treatments: no supplemental feed or interseeded legume (CON), 0.5% BW supplementation with a 50/50 mix of corn gluten feed and soybean hulls (SUP0.5), 1.0% BW supplementation with the same feed mix (SUP1.0), or interseeded red clover (CLOV). Three steers were stocked on each pasture, and additional steers were used in a put-and-take design to manage forage growth. Steers grazed these pastures until active growth ceased (79 and 86 d at BBREC and TVREC, respectively). Data were analyzed using SAS v. 9.4. Results indicated average daily gains were greatest (P < 0.05) from steers receiving 1.0% BW of supplemental feed, followed by 0.5% BW supplemental feed or interseeded red clover, and least from the control. A similar pattern was observed for gain per hectare (P = 0.03). This resulted in different cattle marketing dates across treatments following the study with the byproduct supplemented steers being sold shortly after the trial ended, the steers on the CLOV pastures being sold a month later, and the steers on the CON diet being sold a month and a half after the byproduct supplemented steers. These results are indicative of poor animal performance in the CON treatment and potential tall fescue toxicosis. Thus, the addition of supplemental byproduct feeds and forages can potentially alleviate the growth-inhibiting symptoms of tall fescue toxicosis in beef cattle.
